extracted.intended_audience: authors, copyeditors, proofreaders, and typesetters preparing material for publication (academic/book/journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed style rules for punctuation (brackets, ellipses, hyphens), word divisions, footnotes/indexing, and tabular work intended to guide copyediting and typesetting for formal publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets — permitted uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (1) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given for each use: editorial note in brackets; interpolation in quotations (e.g., 'These [the free-silver Democrats] asserted ...'); rectifying a name within brackets; supplying reference details; and nested parentheses examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketed continuation notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'To be continued' at the end or 'Continued from...' at the beginning of articles/chapters should be placed between brackets, centered, in italics, and set in reduced type in accordance with reduction rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320], [To be concluded]. See cross-reference to reduction/type-size rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses — function and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses indicate omission from a quotation of words not essential to the idea, and to indicate illegible words, mutilations, and other lacunae in quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an ellipsis at beginning/middle/end of a sentence use four periods separated by a space (en-quad), except in very narrow measures. If the preceding line ends in a point, that point is not included in the four. Omitted whole paragraphs or lines (esp. in poetry) should be shown by a full line of periods spaced by em- or 2-em quads, not extending beyond the longest type line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as part of the citation and should be enclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to bracket/quotation guidance (cf. rule 178[3]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen — general uses
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable carried to the next line and between many compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphen acts both for line breaks (divisions) and for linking components in compounds; see specific hyphenation rules for compounds and prefixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity) combined into one adjective preceding a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: well-known author, first-class investment, four-year-old boy, up-to-date machinery. Exceptions: New Testament times; Old English spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use en-dash for complex compounds or components containing multiple words
rubrics_metrics.description: Where such compound words are set in capitals (e.g., headlines), or where one component contains more than one word, use an en-dash instead of a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR; New York–Chicago freight traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate adjective/participle with adverb ending in -ly or when following the noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid hyphenating combinations of adjectives or participles with adverbs ending in '-ly', or when such combinations follow the noun or qualify a predicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: highly developed species; a man well known in the neighborhood; 'Her gown and carriage were strictly up to date.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate noun+noun compounds in objective relation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, hyphenate nouns formed by combining two nouns standing in objective relation (one component derived from a transitive verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, office-holder, hero-worship. Exceptions: common brief compounds like lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate present participle + noun formations
rubrics_metrics.description: Present participle united with a noun to form a new noun (or used absolutely with a preposition) should have a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, working-man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds with book/house/mill/room/shop/work — syllable-based rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'book', 'house', 'mill', 'room', 'shop', 'work' are printed as one word without hyphen when the prefixed noun has one syllable, hyphenated when it contains two syllables, and printed as two separate words when it contains three or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handbook, pocket-book, story-book; boathouse, clubhouse, engine-house; cornmill vs. water-mill; bedroom vs. lecture-room. Exceptions: rare combinations or appearance-based separations (e.g., source-book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation compounds usually hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker', 'dealer', and similar occupation-denoting words should ordinarily be hyphenated, as should nouns denoting multiple occupations of the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer, soldier-statesman. Exceptions: short everyday words like bookmaker, dressmaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation rule for compounds with 'store'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains one syllable; otherwise printed solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but: bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Fellow' compounds always hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are always hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-beings, play-fellow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family-relationship compounds hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of father, mother, brother, sister, daughter, parent, foster (and similar) should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: father-love (but fatherland), mother-tongue, foster-son.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great- (descent) compounds hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great' indicating fourth degree in direct line of descent use a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen (with noted exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but: lifetime), world-power, world-problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Skin' compounds syllable-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with one-syllable words printed as one word; with words of more than one syllable printed as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Master' compounds hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'master' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke (exception: masterpiece).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'God' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds with 'god' use a hyphen in simple formations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sun-god, rain-god.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Half', 'quarter' etc. require hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Half', 'quarter', etc., combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: half-truth, half-tone, quarter-mile, half-title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes 'semi', 'demi', 'bi', 'tri' usually solid
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Semi', 'demi', 'bi', 'tri', etc., do not ordinarily demand a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: semiannual, demigod, biweekly, bipartisan. Exceptions: long or unusual formations such as semi-centennial, demi-relievo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'self' hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds beginning with 'self' are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: self-evident, self-respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations with 'fold' depend on syllables
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations with 'fold' printed as one word if the number is one syllable, as two words if more than one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: twofold, tenfold; fifteen fold, a hundred fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives formed by adding '-like' usually solid or hyphenated by syllable/proper-noun rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives formed with 'like' are usually printed as one word if the noun has one syllable; if the noun contains more (or is a proper noun), they should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: childlike, homelike, godlike; eel-like, bell-like; American-like (but: Christlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of titles linked by hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Vice', 'ex-', 'elect', 'general', and 'lieutenant' as parts of titles should be connected to the chief noun by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vice-Consul Taylor, ex-President Cleveland, the governor-elect, postmaster-general, lieutenant-colonel.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'By-' compounds hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds beginning with 'by-' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: by-product, by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefixes co-, pre-, re-: hyphen if same vowel repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefixes 'co-', 'pre-', and 're-' when followed by the same vowel as that in which they terminate take a hyphen; ordinarily they do not when followed by a different vowel or a consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: co-operation, pre-empted, re-enter; but: coequal, coeducation, prearranged. Note exceptions: proper names, long/unusual formations, and cases where omission would change meaning (e.g., re-cover vs. recover).

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit hyphen in today/tomorrow/tonight/viewpoint/standpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a hyphen in words such as 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'viewpoint,' 'standpoint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-reference to other prefix rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative particles 'un-', 'in-', 'a-' usually solid; 'non-' usually hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: The negative particles 'un-', 'in-', and 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen; 'non-' ordinarily calls for a hyphen except in the commonest words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unmanly, undemocratic, inanimate; non-aesthetic, non-subservient, non-contagious; but: nonage, nondescript, nonessential.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Quasi-' requires hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quasi' prefixed to a noun or adjective requires a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quasi-corporation, quasi-historical.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Over' and 'under' prefixes generally solid
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Over' and 'under' prefixed to a word should not be followed by a hyphen, except in rare cases (lengthy words, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: overbold, overemphasize, underfed; exceptions: over-soul, under-man, over-spiritualistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin prepositional prefixes normally solid
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin prepositions 'ante', 'anti', 'inter', 'intra', 'post', 'sub', 'super' prefixed to a word do not ordinarily require a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: antedate, antechamber, international, submarine. Exceptions: ante-bellum, ante-Nicene, anti-Semitic, inter-university.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Extra', 'infra', 'supra', 'ultra' generally hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Extra', 'infra', 'supra', and 'ultra' as a rule call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extra-hazardous, infra-mundane, supra-temporal, ultra-conservative (but: Ultramontane).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate fractional spelled-out numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect numerator and denominator by a hyphen unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: two-thirds, four and five-sevenths, thirty-hundredths; but: thirty-one hundredths. Do not hyphenate 'one half' in contexts like 'One half of his fortune ...' when phrased that way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted common element indicated by hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together have a common component element, omit that element in all but the last word and indicate the omission by a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen indicates incomplete particle or syllable
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used to indicate a prefix or suffix, as a particle or syllable, not complete in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'The German diminutive suffixes -chen and -lein.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate syllabification
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is employed to indicate the syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: di-a-gram, pho-tog-ra-phy.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common everyday hyphenated words
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain everyday compound words should be hyphenated even if not covered by other classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: after-years, cross-section, man-of-war, son-in-law, bas-relief, death-rate, object-lesson, subject-matter, birth-rate, feast-day, page-proof, thought-process, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary word divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words; wherever consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General admonition to prefer intact words if spacing allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dividing two-letter syllables in wide measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide on a syllable of two letters in wide measures (20 ems or more) if possible; words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'on-ly' should not be divided; 'oc-cur', 'of-fice' rarely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consecutive line endings in hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen if avoidable; avoid dividing the next-to-last line of a paragraph and ensure the last line (breakline) contains at least four letters in measures of 15 ems and up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid divided word at bottom of a right-hand page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns, especially names of persons, unless absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict avoidance emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not separate initials or common abbreviations across lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not separate initials of a name or combinations like A.D., P.M., etc., into different lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep initials and abbreviations intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep divisional mark with its clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the separation of a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (i)) from the section which it precedes; do not allow such a mark to fall at the end of a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry the mark over with the matter it pertains to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide according to pronunciation (American system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide words according to pronunciation, not derivation; as far as compatible with pronunciation and good spacing, divide compounds on etymological lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy (not demo-cracy); dis-pleasure better than displeas-ure; avoid monstrosities like Passo-ver, diso-bedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division when two consonants meet between vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels and the syllable ends on one consonant, the division may be made between the consonants (pronunciation determines place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advan-tage, exces-sive, finan-cier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid terminating line in soft c, g, or j
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not terminate a line in a soft c or g or in a j; escape the division entirely if possible; if not possible, divide following examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred: pro-cess (not proc-ess), ne-cessary (not nec-essary), spacing (not spac-ing). Note: this rule differs from many dictionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide on a vowel wherever practicable; exceptions for -able/-ible
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel when practicable; if a vowel alone forms a syllable in the middle of a word, run it into the first line. Words ending in -able and -ible are exceptions and should carry the vowel over into the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sepa-rate (not sep-arate); read-able (not reada-ble); convert-ible (not converti-ble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated nouns/adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives avoid adding further hyphens when dividing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson (not object-les-son); fellow-being (not fel-low-being).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat diphthongs as single letters for division
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel sounds into one (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; therefore do not divide if avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: peo-ple is a bad division; prefer not to split diphthongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivatives from words ending in consonant with accent shift
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in a consonant, in divisions the consonant should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has been shifted; if the derivative retains the accent of the parent word, the consonant should be left in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject); defect-ive (from defect').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural -s does not justify division
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of a plural s adding a new syllable to words ending in an s-sound does not create an excuse for dividing such words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impossible divisions example: hor-ses and circumstan-ces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives in -ical divided on the 'i'
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives in -ical should be divided on the i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: physi-cal (not phys-ical or physic-al).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide the word 'nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Do not divide nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short prohibition as stated in the manual (literal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing foreign-language words — French
rubrics_metrics.description: French: fundamental principle to divide on a vowel as far as possible, avoiding consonantal endings of syllables; certain consonant combinations and vowel counts/silent e rules apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-te, a-che-ter; tableau (not tab-leau); two consonants where second is s or r carried over: ta-bleau, e-cri-vain. Notice mute 'e' following a vowel does not form a syllable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing foreign-language words — German
rubrics_metrics.description: German: fundamental principle to divide on a vowel; usually only the last of several consonants between vowels is carried over; certain digraphs (sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th) are never separated; ck divides as k-k if necessary; compounds separated along components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hü-ten, Le-ben; Rit-ter; Busze, Be-cher; Deckel — Dek-kel; Fürsten-schloss as component separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing foreign-language words — Italian
rubrics_metrics.description: Italian: divide on a vowel as far as possible; s before a consonant, certain clusters (ch, gh, gli, gn, qu, sc, etc.) are never separated; i and u with following vowels treated specially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-vo-li-no, ca-sti-ghi, miei, tuoi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing foreign-language words — Spanish
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish: divide on a vowel where practicable; ch, ll, rr, ñ and other rules apply (some digraphs treated as simple consonants); certain liquid consonant combinations are not separated except in compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les, mu-cha-cho, ba-ta-lla; sub-lu-nar (exception forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing foreign-language words — Greek
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek: place single consonants, consonant combinations that can begin a word, and mutes followed by liquids at the beginning of a syllable; other consonant combos are divided; compound words are divided into original parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: e-ymo, Trap-a-yw, subject to general rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing foreign-language words — Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin: a word has as many syllables as vowels or diphthongs; divide before a single consonant between vowels; with two or more consonants divide before the last consonant except for certain combinations (mute+liquid, qu, gu); compounds separated first into elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, om-nis, scrip-tus, ad-est, red-e-o.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote reference indices prefer superscript figures
rubrics_metrics.description: For reference indices use superscript figures as a rule; use asterisks, daggers, etc., only in special cases (e.g., tabular or algebraic matter where figures would confuse). Index figures in the text should be placed after punctuation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence when figures are not used: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'ibid.' and abbreviated references in footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ibid.' is used when references to the same work follow each other closely and uninterruptedly, taking the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated; but 'ibid.' should not ordinarily be used for the first footnote on a verso page — repeat title or use loc. cit. or op. cit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples showing full reference then 'Ibid.' and loc. cit. usage; guidance to use sparingly and observe page/placement conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of footnote index after quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to place the index figure in the text after the quotation than before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative reference given earlier in the Footnotes section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit 'Vol., chap., p.' ordinarily in references; numeral conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit 'Vol., chap., and p.' in references to particular passages. Use Roman numerals (capitals) for Volume, Book, Part, and Division (except classical works use lower-case), Roman numerals (lower-case) for chapter and pages of introductory matter, and Arabic numerals for number (Heft) and text pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use 'Vol.' or 'p.' when confusion might arise; examples provided for classical references and English references following classical style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date placement in periodical references
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of publication in a reference to a periodical should immediately follow the volume number and should be put in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex: Journal citations illustrated in footnote examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecutive numbering of footnotes in linotype-set work
rubrics_metrics.description: In linotype-set work, footnotes should be numbered consecutively through an article (in a journal) or through a chapter (in a book) to save resetting in case of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: several journals have adopted different styles — exceptions listed (Botanical Gazette, Astrophysical Journal, Classical Philology, Classical Journal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing — alphabetization of names with particles/prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for arranging names in indexes: French/Belgian/Spanish names with 'le, la, liu, du, des' listed under prefix letters ahead of ordinary L/D list; when preceded by 'de' or 'd'' list under following word with particle placed after initials; if particle is actually part of surname index under particle's initial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Conte, John; La Noüe, François de; De Bey, Robert; De Quincey, Thomas. Further rules for 'von', 'M'/Mac/Me capitalization, 'O', 'St.', 'Van', two-part firm names with 'and/&/y/et/und/e', hyphenated names ordering (English vs. French practice), umlaut treatment, and cross-references reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work — type-size and setting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for type sizes and leading for tables: in 12- and 10-pt matter open tables ordinarily set in 8-pt leaded; ruled in 8-pt solid; in 9-pt matter 8-pt solid, etc. Use different type for columns representing totals/averages/percentages; italic and bold-face figures may be used to set off classes of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed point-size mappings for various body-matter sizes and recommendation for typographic emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular captions and box-heads sizing and case
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. In ruled tables with multi-story box-heads, upper (primary) heads set in caps and small caps, lower (secondary) in caps and lower-case; where small caps used, stub head should also be small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See example and cross-reference to page numbering and figure-only second stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing within ruled tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables, there should be at least two leads' space between horizontal rules and content, and, if practicable, at least equivalent of an en-quad of the body type between vertical rules and enclosed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures readability within box-heads and table cells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leaders or periods in open tables and stubs
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods (one em apart and aligned) or leaders may be used between columns. In ruled tables, leaders should usually be employed in the stub if there is room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition of leader provided and recommendation for when to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blank entries in numeric columns use leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: To express a blank in columns of figures use leaders the width of the largest number in the column (e.g., for four digits use a 2-em leader). Center figures in column; when unequal digit counts leave more space on the left than right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each em contains two dots; use at least two dots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading-matter alignment in table columns
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading-matter in columns of a ruled table, center it if possible; if a line runs over use hanging indentation and align all on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical alignment guidance to preserve neatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double rules and table tops
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables; vertical double rules used usually only when a table is doubled up on itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual formatting convention for distinguishing table headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vs. ruled tables by number of columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables of two columns only should be set as open; tables of three or more columns should be set as ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical layout rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table numbering and headline typography
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Table I' etc. in headlines should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set; the following descriptive line (if any) in caps and small caps of same type. A single descriptive headline without a number should be set in caps of the table type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples shown with specimen tables.
